notes: First-refresh audit, 2026-09-03. One of the two articles the Phase-B batch scheduling orphaned; it had no ledger. The 2026-08-30 emergency strike had already replaced the FABRICATED P.L. 119-75 blockquote with the real SEC. 5005 sentence; that replacement was re-verified character-for-character against data/bill-text/119-HR-7148.txt (L27311-27315) at the start of this session and HOLDS. This audit found three further hard errors the sweep did not: (1) 'any bill ever passed by Congress' is contradicted by Congress.gov's own coverage table, which lists NO available format for bill text from 1874 to 1988; (2) 'Congress.gov publishes every bill, amendment, and committee report' is contradicted by the same table (committee reports start 1995; Senate submitted-amendment full text starts with the 114th Congress); (3) the HEAR Act example dropped the words 'otherwise timely under this Act' - the exact dropped-condition defect the 119-S-1884 bill-lane re-audit had already fixed elsewhere, and which the audited sibling articles/holocaust-art-recovery.html describes as the condition that 'does the limiting work'. The IRS plain-language claim was DELETED, not softened: four irs.gov/treasury.gov candidate URLs all return 404, so the claim is unfetchable (standing rule 3). The SEC claim was re-sourced rather than deleted: the 1998 final rule is real and fetchable from federalregister.gov, and it both states the requirement and announces the handbook. The 300-page/three-provisions/297-provisions arithmetic was invented and is replaced by the real division structure of the Act the article already quotes. ROUND 2 (hostile sonnet pass over the FIXED draft): 2 blocking + 9 advisory returned, and the blocking pair were both defects this session introduced while fixing round 1 - a composite paraphrase presented inside one pair of quotation marks as verbatim statute, and a dropped prong of the covered-document definition. Every one of the 11 was accepted; none was adjudicated away. Also caught and fixed in round 2: six fabricated punctuation-inside-quote marks (the banked two-sided class, checked in both directions), two dropped source hedges, two banned editorial words, four unsourced claims about the public, and an unsourced generalisation about drafting practice replaced by verbatim receipts from Sections 5001 and 5006 of the same Act. 5 U.S.C. 105 was FETCHED and stored to close the one inference the verifier flagged as resting on an unfetched statute. ROUND 3 (a second, independent hostile sonnet pass over the round-2 draft): 5 blocking + 7 advisory. Four of the five blocking findings were ACCEPTED AND FIXED - a false section-adjacency claim ("either side" naming a section four sections away), two non-exhaustive statutory lists rendered as closed enumerations, quotation marks around an unattributed phrase, and two surviving unsourced characterisations of journalism that were the same class as a sentence round 1 had deleted. The fifth, a quoted source missing from both citation lists, was also fixed. One flag was REJECTED with reasons recorded on the ledger: the essay's own thesis sentences are not source-checkable factual assertions. THE LESSON OF THIS ARTICLE IS THAT EACH ROUND'S FIX INTRODUCED THE NEXT ROUND'S DEFECT - round 1 fixed a dropped condition and created a composite quotation; round 2 fixed that and created a false adjacency and a closed list. Three passes, not two, and the third was the one that caught the adjacency error no script could see. ROUND 4 (a third independent hostile sonnet pass): 1 blocking + 5 advisory. The blocking finding is the one that justifies the whole four-round shape - Section 5(f)(1) bars "all defenses OR SUBSTANTIVE DOCTRINES based on the passage of time" and every draft from round 1 through round 3 printed only "all defenses", dropping a whole statutory category on the paragraph the article uses to teach that dropping a qualifier changes the meaning. Three hostile passes had read that paragraph and none caught it, because the ledger row covering it receipted the FACT against a span that contained the dropped words rather than checking the PHRASE the page printed. Fixed, plus a breadcrumb/title mismatch; one flag rejected with reasons. ROUND 5 (a fourth independent hostile sonnet pass): 1 blocking + 5 advisory. The blocking finding was the SAME NARROWING as round 4, one sentence earlier and missed by all four previous passes - "removes a procedural defense" for a provision that bars two categories, one of them expressly "substantive doctrines". Round 4 had seen that sentence and recorded it as noted-not-actioned; that call was wrong and is reversed here. Two advisories accepted as well (three compressed qualifiers in the covered-document definition; two unsourced general rules about drafting turned into observations about the receipted sections). FIVE PASSES ON A 1,100-WORD EXPLAINER, EACH ONE FINDING SOMETHING THE LAST HAD READ AND NOT SEEN. The one structural lesson worth carrying: FOUR of the six blocking findings across rounds 2-5 were the SAME defect class - a restatement quietly narrower than its source - and three of them were introduced by the fix for the previous one. ROUND 6 (a fifth independent hostile sonnet pass): 1 blocking + 1 flagged-for-adjudication + 5 advisory. BOTH of the first two were accepted. The blocking one is the third instance in this article of an unsourced characterisation of the press, in the same section rounds 1 and 3 each cleaned once, sitting two paragraphs from the round-3 fix and carrying no ledger row at any point. The adjudication flag was the ORIGINAL defect of this whole audit - the framing sentence dropped "otherwise timely under this Act" - five rounds after the restatement itself was fixed, and it was caught only because round 5 had just written down the rule that a framing sentence counts. One orphaned ledger row was also found and rewritten: the round-5 prose fix had left a receipt describing prose that no longer existed. SIX PASSES. Each one found something the last five had read. ROUND 7 (a sixth independent hostile sonnet pass): 1 blocking, accepted, plus a self-initiated sweep of the same class across the whole article. Zero new findings in the HEAR Act paragraph and the bill-text section - the two places that produced a defect in five of the six previous rounds - on a pass that re-derived every quotation, every position claim by line number and both word counts from scratch. The finding that did land carries the transferable lesson of this whole audit: THE CLAUSE HAD BEEN IMMUNISED BY A PARTIAL QUOTATION IN AN EARLIER ADJUDICATION. Round 3 recorded a group of thesis sentences as REJECTED and quoted this one only as far as "isn't available at all"; the clause after the colon, which asserts what citizens can and cannot do, was never inside the quoted text and never got a row. Every later pass read a settled adjudication and moved on. An adjudication must quote the WHOLE sentence it is settling, or it silently settles more than it read. ROUND 8 (a seventh independent hostile sonnet pass): 2 blocking, both accepted, plus the advisory that closes the loop round 7 opened. The first blocking finding is the one this article will be remembered for: the "covered document" definition was ASSEMBLED UPSIDE DOWN - the statute's non-exhaustive list of formats was standing where its open substantive test belongs - and rounds 2 and 5 had each edited that exact sentence to restore something dropped from it without either one noticing the structure was inverted. Checking words is not checking structure. The second is the eighth instance of the unsourced-characterisation class, a claim about what reading a bill requires of a reader, which round 5 had adjudicated as thesis voice and which is reversed here. The advisory was to amend the round-3 adjudication to quote its sentences in full; doing so is what makes the difference between the two visible - the closing premise sentence also says something about readers, and it stands, because it declares a premise the publisher holds rather than reporting a fact about the public.

claims.claim: The Plain Writing Act of 2010 requires each agency to use plain writing in every covered document it issues or substantially revises.
claims.sourceSpan: each agency shall use plain writing in every covered document of the agency that the agency issues or substantially revises.

claims.claim: A "covered document" is "any document" that is necessary for obtaining a federal benefit or service or filing taxes, provides information about one, or explains to the public how to comply with a requirement the Federal Government administers or enforces; it includes, in paper or electronic form, a letter, publication, form, notice or instruction, and it does not include a regulation.
claims.sourceSpan: (2) Covered document.--The term ``covered document''-- (A) means any document that-- (i) is necessary for obtaining any Federal Government benefit or service or filing taxes; (ii) provides information about any Federal Government benefit or service; or (iii) explains to the public how to comply with a requirement the Federal Government administers or enforces; (B) includes (whether in paper or electronic form) a letter, publication, form, notice, or instruction; and (C) does not include a regulation.
claims.note: Span widened in round 8 to the WHOLE definition - subparagraphs (A), (B) and (C) together - because the defect the round-7 pass found was structural rather than lexical: a receipt bound to (B) alone cannot show whether the prose has (A) and (B) the right way round.

The article's own worked example of a faithful plain-English restatement read "Laches, adverse possession, and forum non conveniens may no longer be used to dismiss Holocaust art restitution claims, retroactive to cases currently on appeal." It dropped the opening condition of Section 5(f), "With respect to any claim that is otherwise timely under this Act", which is the clause that does the limiting work; and "retroactive to cases currently on appeal" narrowed the applicability provision, which reaches every claim pending in any court on the date of enactment, appeal or not. claims.claim: FLAG REJECTED ON ADJUDICATION. The round-3 verifier flagged the essay's own thesis sentences as unsourced: "The United States has a transparency problem that has nothing to do with classified information."; "It is too low a standard."; "The answer isn't to change how bills are drafted."; and the closing premise sentence IN FULL: "LegislationPatch is built on a specific premise: that the change itself is the story, and that readers are capable of forming their own views about it once they know what it actually says." REJECTED because these are not assertions about the world that a legislative source could confirm or refute - they are the article's stated position, presented as such, on the page that explains why the site exists. The rule this lane enforces is that FACTS come from sources; every empirical, quantitative and attributive claim on the page is receipted above, and every unsourced claim about what other people or institutions actually do was removed in rounds 2 and 3. Also rejected on the same basis: the illustrative hypothetical "change the expiration date", which is offered as an example of what an amendment cannot say, not as a quotation of anything.
claims.sourceSpan: The purpose of this Act is to improve the effectiveness and accountability of Federal agencies to the public by promoting clear Government communication that the public can understand and use.
claims.note: Recorded rather than silently dismissed so the next reader can disagree with the call. Two further round-3 advisories are accepted as noted-not-actioned: the og:description drops the words "of government documents" that the meta description and JSON-LD description carry (pre-existing, cosmetic, three copies of one sentence), and the coverage table's GPO "delays can occur" footnote is not carried into the availability sentence (the sentence claims what is published, not how fast). AMENDED IN ROUND 8, and the amendment is the point. As originally written this row quoted one of its sentences only as far as "isn't available at all" and referred to another as "the closing premise sentence" without quoting it at all. The unquoted remainder of the first - "citizens who can't evaluate what their representatives are doing" - was an unsourced claim about what a real group can do, and it survived six further passes because every reader saw a settled adjudication. The closing premise sentence is now quoted in full, and it is worth seeing why it still stands where the citizens clause did not: it says readers "are capable of forming their own views", inside a sentence that frames itself as a premise the site is built on. That is a normative commitment the publisher is declaring, not an empirical finding about the public - and the difference is visible only when the whole sentence is on the page. AN ADJUDICATION MUST QUOTE EVERY SENTENCE IT SETTLES, IN FULL. ROUND 9: the fourth sentence this row originally listed - "Information that is technically available but functionally inaccessible produces the same political outcome as information that isn't available at all" - no longer exists. Round 7 replaced the whole sentence, including the colon-clause about citizens that this row had immunised, and the finding row finding.r7-citizens-capacity-claim carries that fix. It is dropped from this list rather than re-quoted, because a settled adjudication must not appear to cover prose that is no longer on the page.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 4 - A DROPPED CATEGORY THAT SURVIVED THREE HOSTILE PASSES. Section 5(f)(1) bars "all defenses OR SUBSTANTIVE DOCTRINES based on the passage of time". Rounds 1-3 rendered it as all defenses "based on the passage of time", dropping "or substantive doctrines" and narrowing a two-category bar to one - and the phrase appeared nowhere in the draft (grep returned zero). It matters here specifically: adverse possession, which the same sentence names, is a substantive doctrine that transfers title, not a procedural defense, so the dropped words were doing real work. The prose now quotes the full phrase. The reason it survived is worth recording: the ledger had a row verifying the underlying FACT (that laches and adverse possession may not be applied) against a span that contains the dropped words, but no row checking the fidelity of the PHRASE the article actually printed. A receipt that proves a fact does not prove the wording.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 5 - THE SAME NARROWING, ONE SENTENCE EARLIER, MISSED BY FOUR PASSES. The paragraph introducing the worked example said the bill "removes a procedural defense available to defendants in civil litigation". Section 5(f) bars TWO categories, and the first is expressly "defenses OR SUBSTANTIVE DOCTRINES" - adverse possession and acquisitive prescription, both named in that list, transfer or extinguish title on the merits and are not procedural. The singular "a procedural defense" collapsed two statutory categories into one and mislabelled the half the statute itself distinguishes. Now "removes defenses and doctrines available to defendants in civil litigation". The round-4 ledger had recorded this sentence as noted-not-actioned on the reasoning that the detailed restatement two sentences later carries the right wording; the round-5 verifier disagreed, and it was right to - a framing sentence is a checkable factual claim about what the bill does, not thesis voice.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 7 - THE SEVENTH INSTANCE OF THE UNSOURCED-CHARACTERISATION CLASS, AND THE REASON IT SURVIVED IS THE INTERESTING PART. "Information that is technically available but functionally inaccessible produces the same political outcome as information that is not available at all: citizens who can't evaluate what their representatives are doing." The trailing clause asserts what a real group can and cannot do, which is the same class rounds 1, 3 and 6 each removed once. It survived six passes because the round-3 adjudication quoted that sentence as an example of protected thesis voice AND STOPPED QUOTING AT "isn't available at all" - the clause naming citizens was never inside the quoted text, so every later reader saw a settled adjudication rather than an unchecked claim. AN ADJUDICATION THAT QUOTES ONLY PART OF A SENTENCE IMMUNISES THE REST OF IT. The sentence is now definitional: inaccessible information "leaves a reader in the same position" as unavailable information, which is a statement about the information, not about citizens. In the same edit, "Transparency in government is often described as making information available" - an unsourced assertion that people describe it that way, left standing when round 3 removed only its quotation marks - became "Making information available is one standard of transparency in government."

claims.note: Round 7 also swept the whole article for the class rather than fixing only the flagged instance. The sentences deliberately KEPT, and why: "a reader who cannot read the bill has to rely on someone's account of it instead" (a logical consequence, names no group), "Any account shorter than the bill is selective" (definitional), "A provision like that one is law whether or not anyone writes about it" (a statement about what law is), "Transparency that works only when someone else finds the provision first is incomplete transparency" (definitional, "someone else" names nobody), and "someone who doesn't spend their workday with the U.S. Code" (a hypothetical reader in a design requirement). None asserts what a real group actually does.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 8 - THE DEFINITION WAS BUILT UPSIDE DOWN, AND FOUR EARLIER ROUNDS HAD EDITED THIS EXACT SENTENCE WITHOUT SEEING IT. Section 3(2) defines a covered document in three parts: (A) it "means any document that" meets any of three substantive tests; (B) it "includes (whether in paper or electronic form) a letter, publication, form, notice, or instruction"; (C) it "does not include a regulation". The draft led with the format list - "the letters, publications, forms, notices and instructions a person needs in order to..." - which makes (B) the defining head and demotes (A) to a qualifier on it. That inverts the statute: (A) is an open test that reaches ANY document meeting it, while (B) is a non-exhaustive list of formats those documents come in. As written, a covered document that is none of those five formats read as outside the Act. Round 2 restored a dropped prong of (A) here and round 5 restored three dropped qualifiers here, and neither noticed that the sentence was assembled the wrong way round - both were checking words, not structure. The prose now leads with "any document" and the three tests, and states the formats and the regulation carve-out as what the Act adds.
claims.sourceSpan: (2) Covered document.--The term ``covered document''-- (A) means any document that-- (i) is necessary for obtaining any Federal Government benefit or service or filing taxes; (ii) provides information about any Federal Government benefit or service; or (iii) explains to the public how to comply with a requirement the Federal Government administers or enforces; (B) includes (whether in paper or electronic form) a letter, publication, form, notice, or instruction; and (C) does not include a regulation.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 8 - THE EIGHTH INSTANCE OF THE UNSOURCED-CHARACTERISATION CLASS. "The result is that reading a bill requires either a law degree or a long stretch of time with the U.S. Code open in a separate window." It asserts what reading a bill actually requires of a person - an efficacy claim about readers, no source, and no ledger row at any point across seven passes. Round 5 saw it and recorded it as thesis voice; that call is reversed here on the same reasoning round 5 itself established for framing sentences. Replaced with a statement about the document instead of about the reader: "The result is that the meaning of the sentence is not in the sentence. It is in Section 225(e) of the Act the sentence names, which the sentence does not reproduce." Both halves are visible in the receipted blockquote - it cites Section 225(e) and does not quote it.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 9 - THE TWO-SIDED PUNCTUATION RULE, CAUGHT ON THE OTHER SIDE THIS TIME. Round 2 moved six marks OUT of closing quotes because their source sentences did not end there. The round-8 rewrite of the covered-document paragraph then set two marks outside where the source sentence DOES end: "...that the agency issues or substantially revises." and "(C) does not include a regulation." Both verified by byte comparison this session - the character immediately after each quoted fragment in the stored Act is a period, and the next token begins a new subsection. Both periods moved INSIDE. The rule is two-sided and this article has now been corrected in both directions, which is the point of stating it that way.
